messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 72
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Network Engineer
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 36

**Patient:** Ms. Evelyn R., age 72
**Occupation:** Network Engineer (retired, but works part-time as a consultant)
**Trauma:** Witnessing a fatal workplace accident

Evelyn is a lean, sharp-eyed woman who sits with her back perfectly straight, as if she’s bracing for a server crash. She retired from her full-time role as a network engineer three years ago, but she still consults two days a week for a regional telecom company. Her mind, she says, is still the fastest thing in the room. But lately, it feels like the whole system is running on faulty wiring.

The event happened six months ago. She was in the main data center, a cold, humming room full of blinking blue lights, running a routine diagnostic. A junior technician, a young man named Derek who always brought her black coffee, was working on a ladder near the overhead cable trays. He was twenty-six, engaged, and had a laugh that filled the whole floor. Evelyn heard a metallic screech, then a sickening crack. She looked up just as the fiberglass ladder buckled. Derek fell twelve feet, landing on the concrete floor with a sound she had never heard before and cannot unhear. She was the first person to reach him. She held his hand while another engineer called 911. He was conscious, but his leg was bent at an impossible angle, and he kept whispering, “I’m sorry, I’m sorry.” He died of a brain bleed three hours later at the hospital.

Evelyn did not cry at work. She helped secure the scene, wrote the incident report, and went home. That night, she woke up at 3:17 a.m. gasping, her hands numb, her heart slamming against her ribs. She thought she was having a heart attack. Her husband, Tom, drove her to the ER. Tests were normal. The doctor said “anxiety.”

Now, Evelyn avoids the data center. She asks her colleagues to meet her in the break room or a conference room, which she knows is inefficient. She cannot look at a ladder without her throat closing. Last week, her grandson asked her to help him change a lightbulb in the garage. She told him she was too tired, then locked herself in the bathroom and cried for twenty minutes.

Her sleep is shattered. She dreams of the sound—the crack—and of Derek’s voice saying “I’m sorry.” She wakes up checking her own pulse. She has started drinking two glasses of wine every night to get to sleep, then waking up at 3:17 a.m. on the dot, as if her body has its own alarm clock.

The hardest part, she tells me, is the guilt. She is a problem-solver. She has spent forty years building redundant systems, designing fail-safes, ensuring uptime. She could not save Derek. In her mind, she replays the scene over and over, looking for the variable she missed. Should she have checked the ladder herself? Should she have insisted on a different safety protocol? She knows, logically, that she is not responsible. But logic, she says, is no longer running the system.

At work, she is still competent. She can troubleshoot a routing issue in minutes. But the moment she hears a loud noise—a dropped tool, a door slamming—her vision tunnels, and she feels a cold sweat break out on her back. She has started working from home more, claiming she needs quiet for a complex project. Tom is patient, but he is worried. He says she is not the same person.

She is not. Evelyn was always the one who stayed calm in a crisis. Now, she feels like a computer running on a corrupted hard drive. She knows the data is there, but the retrieval is broken. She wants to be fixed. She wants to go back to the data center without her heart pounding. She wants to sleep through the night. She wants to stop hearing Derek’s voice. But she does not know how to reboot.
